views.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Hold the current matching $50 billion tariff posture and keep the already-announced $60 billion contingent list in reserve until Washington actually implements List 3. Do not fire first, do not offer unrequited purchase commitments or Made in China 2025 concessions, and do not open a non-tariff front against U.S. firms operating in China. Keep a working-level channel open, but treat further talks as exploratory only until a senior U.S. counterpart can actually bind the White House.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: The threat reading is high but not existential. Lists 1 and 2 are already in force at 25 percent on ~$50 billion, aimed at aerospace, ICT, robotics and other Made in China 2025 sectors (timeline 2018-06-15, 2018-07-06, 2018-08-23). USTR’s proposed List 3 (~$200 billion, ~6,000 lines) closed public comment on 5 September, with the rate under review at 10 or 25 percent, and the President has threatened a further tranche that would cover essentially all remaining Chinese goods. That combination, plus the April ZTE denial order that nearly shut a national champion, is a material hit to export interests and a demonstrated firm-level vulnerability. FX pressure is already visible: USD/CNY moved from about 6.30 in April to 6.83 on 5 September (~8 percent), monthly average 6.86, and PBOC raised the mid-point sharply in late August to put a floor under the currency. Reserves slipped only modestly (about $3.14T to $3.11T). The case is not +0.5/+1.0 because industrial production is still +5.8 percent y/y, seasonally adjusted merchandise exports are still rising, ZTE’s ban was lifted on 13 July after a $1.4 billion settlement, and List 3 is not yet in force.

The action stance is a near-zero hold, not a fresh escalation or a concession. China already matched the completed $50 billion package dollar-for-dollar and on 3 August published a contingent 5–25 percent list on ~$60 billion of U.S. goods if List 3 proceeds; implementing that list only after the U.S. move is the proportional reply, not a new decision today. Going beyond it (rare-earth or regulatory measures against U.S. firms, or weaponizing the yuan) would likely give Washington a pretext for the threatened next $200 billion / ~$500 billion tranche and more export-control actions, while China has almost no remaining U.S. goods left to tariff like-for-like. Unilateral purchases already failed: the 19 May joint statement was repudiated on 29 May, and the 22–23 August Wang–Malpass talks produced no schedule and no structural meeting of minds. U.S. List 3 hearings had to be doubled under industry opposition and Senate Finance Chair Hatch called the $200 billion list reckless — that domestic friction is more useful if Beijing does not over-escalate. Therefore hold: keep the $60 billion list ready, refuse structural giveaways, and do not escalate first.
key_factors: List 1+2 already in force at 25% on $50B targeting MIC 2025 sectors; China has already matched
List 3 ($200B, possibly 25%) comment period closed 5 Sep and is imminent but not yet imposed; Trump has threatened a further all-goods tranche
CNY down ~8% since April with late-August PBOC support; reserves only slightly lower — FX pressure real, not a 2015-style run
ZTE denial order showed lethal export-control leverage, but the ban was lifted 13 Jul on punitive settlement terms
May purchase truce collapsed in 10 days; Aug 22–23 talks were mid-level, produced no follow-up, and the U.S. still demands structural MIC 2025 changes China will not give
China cannot match List 3 dollar-for-dollar; the $60B contingent list is the remaining tariff capacity and should stay contingent
U.S. real economy still firm (sentiment 100.1, low VIX) while U.S. firms and some Republicans are pushing back on List 3 — over-escalation would waste that friction

sources_cited.excerpt: List 2 tariffs take effect: US 25% on ~$16B (completing the $50B package). China imposes matching ~$16B retaliation.
USTR publishes proposed List 3: ~$200B of Chinese imports for an additional 10% tariff (~6,000 product lines).
At Trump's direction, USTR says it is considering raising the proposed List 3 rate from 10% to 25%.
US and China release joint statement after talks: China agrees to "significantly increase" purchases of US goods and services. Mnuchin says trade war is "on hold."
White House announces the US will proceed with Section 301 actions, including 25% tariffs on ~$50B of Chinese imports. Truce collapses.
US Commerce Department bans ZTE from buying US components (denial order). ZTE faces operational shutdown. Major non-tariff escalation.
CNY/USD 6.327 on 2018-03-12 to 6.827 on 2018-09-05 (~8% depreciation); monthly average 6.8551 in September.
China industrial production still +5.8% y/y as of 2018-09-01, slowing from 107.0 in April but not contracting.
China reserves excluding gold ~$3.106T on 2018-09-01, down about 1.2% over the window — orderly, not a reserve crisis.
China announced 5–25% duties on $60B / 5,207 U.S. products if the U.S. proceeds with the $200B list.
Aug 22–23 Wang–Malpass talks ended with no breakthrough and no further talks scheduled.
Commerce lifted the ZTE denial order after $1B penalty, $400M escrow, leadership overhaul and 10-year monitors.
USTR doubled List 3 hearings to six days; 359 witnesses; tariffs expected after comment period ending early September.
PBOC raised the yuan mid-point by the most in nearly 15 months in late August to put a floor under the currency.
